title: Basics in R: Part-2 (Data cleaning)
text:
Missing Data Handling
Missing data are common in real-world datasets and can arise for many reasons, including nonresponse, data-entry errors, skipped survey questions, equipment failure, or loss to follow-up. How missing data are handled can have an important effect on the results of an analysis.
Therefore, missing observations should not automatically be deleted or replaced without first considering why the data are missing and how the missingness may affect the research question.
In R, missing values are commonly represented by NA. Empty strings ("") may also occur in character variables and can represent missing information, although they are not automatically treated as NA by R.
This chapter introduces several approaches to identifying and handling missing data. We will focus on:

Identifying and removing missing values
Constant value imputation
Mean and median imputation
Model-based imputation
Multiple imputation
Choosing an appropriate missing-data strategy


Identifying and Handling misisng or Blank Values
Before deciding how to handle missing data, the first step is to identify where missing observations occur.
Let us begin by creating two simple vectors. The first contains an empty string, while the second contains an NA value.

blanks <- c("John", "Jane", "")
nas <- c(NA, "Jane", "Joe")

print(blanks)

#> [1] "John" "Jane" ""

print(nas)

#> [1] NA     "Jane" "Joe"



Identifying NA Values
The is.na() function identifies missing values represented by NA.

is.na(nas)

#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE


The result is a logical vector containing TRUE and FALSE values. A TRUE value indicates that the corresponding observation is missing.
We can use is.na() to extract only the missing observations:

only_nas <- nas[is.na(nas)]

print(only_nas)

#> [1] NA


More commonly, we want to retain observations that are not missing. The ! operator means “not.”

no_nas <- nas[!is.na(nas)]

print(no_nas)

#> [1] "Jane" "Joe"


Thus:

is.na(x) identifies missing observations, while
!is.na(x) identifies observations that are not missing.



Identifying Blank Strings
An empty string ("") is different from NA.
We can identify empty strings using the equality operator ==.

blanks == ""

#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE


We can extract only the blank observations:

only_blanks <- blanks[blanks == ""]

print(only_blanks)

#> [1] ""


Similarly, we can retain observations that are not blank:

no_blanks <- blanks[blanks != ""]

print(no_blanks)

#> [1] "John" "Jane"


It is often useful to convert blank strings to NA so that all missing observations can be handled consistently.

blanks[blanks == ""] <- NA

print(blanks)

#> [1] "John" "Jane" NA


We can now use is.na() to identify these observations:

is.na(blanks)

#> [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE




Counting Missing Values
Before deciding how to handle missing data, it is useful to determine how many missing observations exist.
For a vector, we can use:

sum(is.na(nas))

#> [1] 1


The proportion of missing observations can be calculated using:

mean(is.na(nas))

#> [1] 0.3333333


For a data frame, colSums() can be used to count missing observations in each variable.

students <- c("John", "Jane", "Joe", "Janet")
scores <- c(100, 80, NA, 90)
age <- c(20, NA, 22, 21)

df <- data.frame(
  student = students,
  score = scores,
  age = age
)

print(df)

#>   student score age
#> 1    John   100  20
#> 2    Jane    80  NA
#> 3     Joe    NA  22
#> 4   Janet    90  21


Count the number of missing values in each variable:

colSums(is.na(df))

#> student   score     age 
#>       0       1       1


Calculate the percentage of missing values:

colMeans(is.na(df)) * 100

#> student   score     age 
#>       0      25      25




Removing Observations with Missing Values
One simple approach to missing data is to remove observations containing missing values.
The na.omit() function removes rows containing one or more NA values.

students <- c("John", "Jane", "Joe")
scores <- c(100, 80, NA)

df <- data.frame(
  student = students,
  score = scores
)

print(df)

#>   student score
#> 1    John   100
#> 2    Jane    80
#> 3     Joe    NA


Remove observations containing missing values:

df_complete <- na.omit(df)

print(df_complete)

#>   student score
#> 1    John   100
#> 2    Jane    80


Although na.omit() is convenient, deleting observations should not automatically be the default approach.
If missingness is related to characteristics of the participants or variables being studied, complete-case analysis can introduce bias.



Constant Value Imputation
Constant value imputation replaces missing observations with a predetermined value.
For example:

students <- c("John", "Jane", "Joe")
scores <- c(100, 80, NA)

df <- data.frame(
  student = students,
  score = scores
)

print(df)

#>   student score
#> 1    John   100
#> 2    Jane    80
#> 3     Joe    NA


If we know that the missing value represents a score of zero, we can replace it with 0:

df$score[is.na(df$score)] <- 0

print(df)

#>   student score
#> 1    John   100
#> 2    Jane    80
#> 3     Joe     0


However, researchers should be careful when using zero as an imputation value.
A missing value and a zero value are not necessarily the same thing.
For example:

0 hospital visits means that the person had no hospital visits.
NA hospital visits means that the number of visits is unknown.

Therefore, zero should only be used when there is a substantive reason to believe that the missing value represents zero.

Mean Imputation
Another simple approach is to replace missing values with the mean of the observed values.
Suppose we have data on the number of hours employees spend performing a particular task:

employees <- c("John", "Jane", "Joe", "Janet")
hours_spent <- c(12, 14, NA, 9)

df <- data.frame(
  employee = employees,
  hours_spent = hours_spent
)

print(df)

#>   employee hours_spent
#> 1     John          12
#> 2     Jane          14
#> 3      Joe          NA
#> 4    Janet           9


Calculate the mean using:

mean_value <- mean(
  df$hours_spent,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

print(mean_value)

#> [1] 11.66667


Replace the missing observation with the mean:

df$hours_spent[
  is.na(df$hours_spent)
] <- mean_value

print(df)

#>   employee hours_spent
#> 1     John    12.00000
#> 2     Jane    14.00000
#> 3      Joe    11.66667
#> 4    Janet     9.00000


Mean imputation is easy to implement but has important limitations. When multiple missing observations are replaced with the same mean:

variability in the data is reduced;
the distribution may be distorted;
relationships between variables may be weakened; and
standard errors may be underestimated.

Therefore, mean imputation is generally not recommended as the primary approach for substantial missing data in inferential analyses.


Median Imputation
The median can also be used to replace missing values.
Median imputation may be useful when a variable is highly skewed or contains extreme values.
Reset the variable:

df$hours_spent <- hours_spent

print(df)

#>   employee hours_spent
#> 1     John          12
#> 2     Jane          14
#> 3      Joe          NA
#> 4    Janet           9


Calculate the median:

median_value <- median(
  df$hours_spent,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

print(median_value)

#> [1] 12


Replace the missing observation:

df$hours_spent[
  is.na(df$hours_spent)
] <- median_value

print(df)

#>   employee hours_spent
#> 1     John          12
#> 2     Jane          14
#> 3      Joe          12
#> 4    Janet           9


Median imputation is simple and less sensitive to extreme values than mean imputation. However, it still does not account for uncertainty surrounding the missing value and can distort relationships between variables.



Model-Based Imputation
Instead of replacing all missing observations with the same value, we can use information from other variables to estimate missing values.
For example, consider two variables, x and y:

y <- c(10, 8, NA, 9, 4, NA)
x <- c(8, 6, 9, 7, 2, 12)

df <- data.frame(
  y = y,
  x = x
)

print(df)

#>    y  x
#> 1 10  8
#> 2  8  6
#> 3 NA  9
#> 4  9  7
#> 5  4  2
#> 6 NA 12


The outcome variable y contains two missing observations, while x is observed for every individual.
We can use linear regression to model the relationship between x and y:

model <- lm(
  y ~ x,
  data = df
)

summary(model)

#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = y ~ x, data = df)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#> 1 2 4 5 
#> 0 0 0 0 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)        2          0     Inf   <2e-16 ***
#> x                  1          0     Inf   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 0 on 2 degrees of freedom
#>   (2 observations deleted due to missingness)
#> Multiple R-squared:      1,  Adjusted R-squared:      1 
#> F-statistic:   Inf on 1 and 2 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


We can use the fitted model to predict values of y for observations where y is missing:

missing_y <- is.na(df$y)

imputed_values <- predict(
  model,
  newdata = data.frame(
    x = df$x[missing_y]
  )
)

print(imputed_values)

#>  1  2 
#> 11 14


Insert the predicted values into the missing positions:

df$y[missing_y] <- imputed_values

print(df)

#>    y  x
#> 1 10  8
#> 2  8  6
#> 3 11  9
#> 4  9  7
#> 5  4  2
#> 6 14 12


This approach is more informative than replacing every missing value with the overall mean because the imputed value depends on information from another variable.
However, this is single model-based imputation, not true multiple imputation.


Multiple Imputation
Multiple imputation is a more advanced approach to handling missing data.
Instead of creating one completed dataset, multiple imputation creates several datasets in which missing values are replaced with plausible values.
Each completed dataset is then analyzed separately, and the results are combined.
The basic process is:

Identify missing observations.
Create multiple plausible versions of the missing values.
Analyze each completed dataset.
Combine the estimates.
Incorporate uncertainty caused by missing data.

One commonly used R package for multiple imputation is mice.

library(mice)

Create a dataset containing missing values:

set.seed(123)

dat <- data.frame(
  age = c(25, 31, NA, 45, 52, 38, NA, 29),
  bmi = c(22.1, 25.4, 27.8, NA, 31.2, 24.8, 29.1, NA),
  systolic_bp = c(
    118, 125, 130, 145,
    NA, 128, 140, 119
  )
)

print(dat)

#>   age  bmi systolic_bp
#> 1  25 22.1         118
#> 2  31 25.4         125
#> 3  NA 27.8         130
#> 4  45   NA         145
#> 5  52 31.2          NA
#> 6  38 24.8         128
#> 7  NA 29.1         140
#> 8  29   NA         119


We can examine the missing-data pattern:

md.pattern(dat)








#>   systolic_bp age bmi  
#> 3           1   1   1 0
#> 2           1   1   0 1
#> 2           1   0   1 1
#> 1           0   1   1 1
#>             1   2   2 5


Perform multiple imputation:

imp <- mice(
  dat,
  m = 5,
  method = "pmm",
  seed = 123
)

#> 
#>  iter imp variable
#>   1   1  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   1   2  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   1   3  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   1   4  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   1   5  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   2   1  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   2   2  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   2   3  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   2   4  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   2   5  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   3   1  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   3   2  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   3   3  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   3   4  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   3   5  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   4   1  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   4   2  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   4   3  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   4   4  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   4   5  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   5   1  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   5   2  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   5   3  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   5   4  age  bmi  systolic_bp
#>   5   5  age  bmi  systolic_bp


Here:

m = 5 creates five imputed datasets.
method = "pmm" uses predictive mean matching.
seed = 123 ensures reproducibility.

We can inspect the first completed dataset:

completed_data <- complete(
  imp,
  1
)

print(completed_data)

#>   age  bmi systolic_bp
#> 1  25 22.1         118
#> 2  31 25.4         125
#> 3  25 27.8         130
#> 4  45 27.8         145
#> 5  52 31.2         140
#> 6  38 24.8         128
#> 7  38 29.1         140
#> 8  29 22.1         119


We can also obtain all completed datasets:

complete(
  imp,
  "all"
)

#> $`1`
#>   age  bmi systolic_bp
#> 1  25 22.1         118
#> 2  31 25.4         125
#> 3  25 27.8         130
#> 4  45 27.8         145
#> 5  52 31.2         140
#> 6  38 24.8         128
#> 7  38 29.1         140
#> 8  29 22.1         119
#> 
#> $`2`
#>   age  bmi systolic_bp
#> 1  25 22.1         118
#> 2  31 25.4         125
#> 3  45 27.8         130
#> 4  45 24.8         145
#> 5  52 31.2         128
#> 6  38 24.8         128
#> 7  45 29.1         140
#> 8  29 22.1         119
#> 
#> $`3`
#>   age  bmi systolic_bp
#> 1  25 22.1         118
#> 2  31 25.4         125
#> 3  45 27.8         130
#> 4  45 27.8         145
#> 5  52 31.2         130
#> 6  38 24.8         128
#> 7  38 29.1         140
#> 8  29 29.1         119
#> 
#> $`4`
#>   age  bmi systolic_bp
#> 1  25 22.1         118
#> 2  31 25.4         125
#> 3  31 27.8         130
#> 4  45 25.4         145
#> 5  52 31.2         145
#> 6  38 24.8         128
#> 7  29 29.1         140
#> 8  29 22.1         119
#> 
#> $`5`
#>   age  bmi systolic_bp
#> 1  25 22.1         118
#> 2  31 25.4         125
#> 3  52 27.8         130
#> 4  45 31.2         145
#> 5  52 31.2         145
#> 6  38 24.8         128
#> 7  45 29.1         140
#> 8  29 29.1         119
#> 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "mild" "list"




Analyzing Multiply Imputed Data
The completed datasets should not simply be combined into one large dataset.
Instead, the analysis is performed separately within each imputed dataset, and the results are then pooled.
For example, suppose we want to model systolic blood pressure as a function of age and BMI:

fit <- with(
  imp,
  lm(
    systolic_bp ~ age + bmi
  )
)

The results can then be pooled:

pooled_results <- pool(fit)

summary(pooled_results)

#>          term   estimate  std.error statistic       df   p.value
#> 1 (Intercept) 88.0628836 39.4219110 2.2338563 1.166318 0.2386250
#> 2         age  0.6924738  0.5526748 1.2529498 1.771319 0.3504498
#> 3         bmi  0.5988944  2.1725796 0.2756605 1.034357 0.8275871


Pooling accounts for:

uncertainty within each completed dataset; and
uncertainty caused by the missing data.

This is one of the major advantages of multiple imputation over simple mean or median imputation.


Missing Data Mechanisms
The appropriate missing-data method depends partly on why the data are missing.
Three commonly discussed missing-data mechanisms are described below.

Missing Completely at Random (MCAR)
Data are missing completely at random (MCAR) when the probability of an observation being missing is unrelated to both observed and unobserved data.
For example, suppose several laboratory samples are accidentally lost because of a random equipment failure, with no relationship to participant characteristics.
Under MCAR, complete-case analysis may produce unbiased estimates, although it reduces the available sample size.


Missing at Random (MAR)
Data are missing at random (MAR) when missingness is related to variables that have been observed. For example, suppose younger participants are less likely to report income. If age is available for everyone, the relationship between age and missing income can potentially be incorporated into an imputation model.
Many multiple-imputation methods rely on the MAR assumption.


Missing Not at Random (MNAR)
Data are missing not at random (MNAR) when the probability of missingness depends on information that remains unobserved. For example, individuals with particularly high incomes may be less likely to report their income because their income is high.
MNAR is more difficult to address because the information related to missingness is itself unavailable. Sensitivity analyses and specialized missing-data models may therefore be necessary.



Choosing an Appropriate Missing-Data Method
There is no single missing-data method that is appropriate for every dataset.







Situation
Possible approach




Missing value genuinely represents zero
Constant-value imputation


Very small amount of MCAR missingness
Complete-case analysis


Simple exploratory analysis
Mean or median imputation


Missingness related to observed variables
Multiple imputation


Complex epidemiological analysis
Carefully specified multiple imputation


Suspected MNAR mechanism
Sensitivity analysis or specialized models



The decision should consider:

Amount of missing data
Pattern of missingness
Type of variable
Study design
Analysis model
Plausible missing-data mechanism
Potential for missingness to introduce systematic bias.



Practical Recommendations
When working with missing data in R, the following workflow is recommended.
Step 1: Identify Missing Values

is.na(df)

Step 2: Count Missing Values

colSums(is.na(df))

Step 3: Calculate the Percentage of Missing Values

colMeans(is.na(df)) * 100

Step 4: Check for Other Missing-Value Codes
Some datasets use values such as:

""
"."
"99"
"999"

These should only be treated as missing when the study documentation or codebook confirms that they represent missing information.
For example:

df$variable[df$variable %in% c("", ".", "99", "999")] <- NA

Step 5: Examine the Pattern of Missingness
For datasets with multiple variables, examine which variables tend to be missing together.

md.pattern(df)

Step 6: Consider Why the Data Are Missing
Ask whether the missingness is likely to be:

MCAR
MAR or
MNAR.

Step 7: Select an Appropriate Method
Do not automatically remove observations or replace missing values with zero.
Consider multiple imputation when appropriate.
Step 8: Perform Sensitivity Analyses
When conclusions may depend on assumptions about missingness, perform sensitivity analyses using alternative reasonable assumptions.
Step 9: Document the Method
Clearly report: - how much data were missing? - which variables contained missing data? - how missingness was assessed? - the method used to handle missing data. - variables included in the imputation model - the number of imputations - assumptions about missingness and - any sensitivity analyses performed.


Resources for Missing data handling

https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/arm/missing.pdf

Types of Data
Data collected in biostatistics and epidemiology generally fall into two broad categories: qualitative (categorical) and quantitative (numerical) data.

title: Types of data and scales of measurement
text:
Qualitative (Categorical) Data
Categorical data represent characteristics or attributes that place individuals into groups or categories. They cannot be meaningfully added, subtracted, or averaged.

Nominal data: Categories with no inherent order. Example: blood type (A, B, AB, O), sex, marital status, country of residence, vaccination status (vaccinated/unvaccinated).
Ordinal data: Categories with a meaningful order, but the intervals between categories are not necessarily equal. Example: cancer stage (I, II, III, IV), pain severity (mild, moderate, severe), socioeconomic status (low, middle, high), Likert scale responses (strongly disagree to strongly agree).



Quantitative (Numerical) Data
Numerical data represent measurable quantities and can be manipulated arithmetically.

Discrete data: Data that can take only specific, countable values (usually whole numbers), typically arising from counting. Example: number of children per household, number of hospital admissions per day, number of new COVID-19 cases per week, parity (number of live births).
Continuous data: Data that can take any value within a range, typically arising from measurement. Example: height, weight, blood pressure, serum cholesterol level, BMI, gestational age.







A useful rule of thumb: if you can meaningfully ask “how many?” the data are usually discrete; if you can ask “how much?” and fractional values make sense, the data are usually continuous.

Variables
A variable is any characteristic, number, or quantity that can be measured or counted and that can differ from one individual (or observation) to another.

Classification of Variables

Independent variable (exposure/predictor): The variable believed to influence or predict the outcome. Example: smoking status.
Dependent variable (outcome/response): The variable being predicted or explained. Example: lung cancer status.
Confounding variable: A variable associated with both the exposure and the outcome that can distort the observed association if not controlled for. Example: age as a confounder in the relationship between physical activity and heart disease.

Public health example: In a study of the relationship between air pollution (independent variable measured as PM2.5 concentration, a continuous variable) and asthma attacks (dependent variable, a discrete count), age and smoking status might act as confounding variables.

Scales of Measurement
Stanley Smith Stevens (1946) classified measurement into four scales(Stevens 1946). Understanding the scale of measurement of a variable is essential because it determines which descriptive statistics and which statistical tests are appropriate.

A simple test for ratio scale: does “zero” mean “none of the quantity,” and does it make sense to say “20 kg is twice as heavy as 10 kg”? If yes, it is a ratio scale. Temperature in Celsius fails this test (0°C is not “no temperature,” and 20°C is not “twice as hot” as 10°C), so it is only an interval scale.



Nominal and ordinal scales are collectively referred to as categorical, while interval and ratio scales are collectively referred to as numerical/quantitative. Most public health and clinical measurements (weight, blood pressure, cell counts, survival time) are on the ratio scale.

title: Estimation
text:
Estimation
Estimation is the process of using sample data to infer the value of an unknown population parameter. When estimating an unknown population parameter, different estimators may perform differently. A good estimator is one that provides estimates that are close to the true population parameter and behaves reliably across repeated samples. Four important properties commonly used to evaluate an estimator are unbiasedness, efficiency, consistency, and sufficiency.

title: Estimation
text:
Unbiasedness
An estimator is said to be unbiased if its expected value is equal to the true population parameter.
If \(\hat{\theta}\) is an estimator of a population parameter \(\theta\), then \(\hat{\theta}\) is unbiased if
\[
E(\hat{\theta}) = \theta.
\]
In other words, an unbiased estimator does not systematically overestimate or underestimate the population parameter. Across many repeated samples, the average of the estimates will equal the true parameter.
For example, the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is an unbiased estimator of the population mean \(\mu\):
\[
E(\bar{X}) = \mu.
\]


2. Efficiency
Efficiency refers to the precision of an estimator. Among unbiased estimators of the same population parameter, the estimator with the smaller variance is generally considered more efficient.
For an estimator \(\hat{\theta}\), its variance measures how much the estimates vary from sample to sample:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\theta}).
\]
A smaller variance means that repeated estimates tend to be more closely clustered around the true population parameter.
For example, when estimating the population mean under the usual assumptions, the sample mean is more efficient than estimators such as the sample median because the sample mean generally has a smaller sampling variance.

In simple terms: An efficient estimator provides more precise estimates with less sampling variability.

Efficiency should not be confused with unbiasedness. An estimator can be unbiased but less efficient than another unbiased estimator.


3. Consistency
An estimator is consistent if it gets closer to the true population parameter as the sample size increases.
More formally, an estimator \(\hat{\theta}_n\) is consistent for \(\theta\) if
\[
\hat{\theta}_n \xrightarrow{P} \theta
\quad \text{as} \quad n \rightarrow \infty,
\]
where \(\xrightarrow{P}\) denotes convergence in probability.
In practical terms, as more observations are collected, the probability that the estimator differs substantially from the true population parameter becomes increasingly small.
For example, the sample mean is a consistent estimator of the population mean. As the sample size increases, the sample mean generally gets closer to the population mean.

Key idea: Consistency concerns what happens as the sample size becomes very large.



4. Sufficiency
An estimator is sufficient if it contains all the information in the sample that is relevant to estimating a particular population parameter.
More formally, a statistic \(T(X)\) is sufficient for a parameter \(\theta\) if, once \(T(X)\) is known, the remaining information in the sample provides no additional information about \(\theta\).
The factorization theorem provides a useful mathematical criterion for determining whether a statistic is sufficient. If the likelihood can be written as
\[
L(\theta \mid x) = g(T(x),\theta)h(x),
\]
then \(T(x)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).
For example, for a random sample from a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda\), the sum
\[
T = \sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i
\]
is a sufficient statistic for \(\lambda\). Once the total number of observed events is known, the individual arrangement of those observations provides no additional information about \(\lambda\).

Key idea: Sufficiency means that the statistic captures all the information about the parameter contained in the sample.



Summary of the Criteria








Property
Main idea
Question it answers




Unbiasedness
\(E(\hat{\theta}) = \theta\)
Does the estimator systematically over- or underestimate?


Efficiency
Smaller variance among comparable estimators
How precise is the estimator?


Consistency
\(\hat{\theta}\) approaches \(\theta\) as \(n\) increases
Does the estimator improve with larger samples?


Sufficiency
Retains all information about the parameter
Does the statistic contain all relevant information from the sample?









Remember



Unbiasedness = correct on average
Efficiency = precise
Consistency = improves with increasing sample size
Sufficiency = retains all relevant information

title: Estimation
text:
Point Estimation
A point estimate is a single numeric value, calculated from sample data, that serves as the “best guess” for a population parameter.







Population Parameter
Point Estimator (Sample Statistic)




\(\mu\) (population mean)
\(\bar{x}\) (sample mean)


\(\sigma^2\) (population variance)
\(s^2\) (sample variance)


\(\pi\) or \(P\) (population proportion)
\(\hat{p}\) (sample proportion)



Desirable properties of a good point estimator: unbiasedness (its expected value equals the true parameter, e.g., \(E(\bar{x})=\mu\)), consistency (it converges to the true parameter as \(n\to\infty\)), and efficiency (it has the smallest possible variance among unbiased estimators).






A point estimate alone gives no information about its precision or reliability. A sample mean of \(\bar{x}=126\) mmHg conveys nothing about how much uncertainty surrounds that estimate. Was it based on 10 patients or 10,000? Interval estimation solves this problem.

title: Estimation
text:
Standard Error
The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic — it quantifies how much a sample statistic (like \(\bar{x}\)) would vary from sample to sample if we repeated the sampling process many times.
\[SE(\bar{x}) = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \qquad SE(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}\]






Do not confuse standard deviation (SD) with standard error (SE). The SD describes variability of individual observations in the data; the SE describes variability of the sample statistic itself (e.g., the mean) across repeated samples. As \(n\) increases, SD stays roughly constant (it reflects the population), but SE shrinks (larger samples give more precise/stable estimates of the mean), because \(SE = s/\sqrt{n}\).

title: Estimation
section: Interval Estimation and the Confidence Interval
text:
Interval Estimation and the Confidence Interval

Definition
A confidence interval (CI) is a range of values, calculated from sample data, that is likely to contain the true population parameter, along with a stated confidence level (e.g., 95%) reflecting the long-run reliability of the method used to construct it.


General Formula
\[\text{Point estimate} \pm (\text{Critical value}) \times (\text{Standard error})\] where,
\(Margin.of.error(ME)=critical.value \times standard.error\)


Confidence Interval for a Mean
When \(\sigma\) is unknown, we use \(t\) statistics,
\[\bar{x} \pm t_{\alpha/2, n-1} \times \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]


Confidence Interval for a Proportion
\[\hat{p} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\times\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}\]

title: Estimation
text:
Margin of Error
The margin of error (ME) is the “plus-or-minus” part of the confidence interval: \[ME = (\text{Critical value})\times(\text{Standard error})\]
A larger margin of error means a wider, less precise interval; margin of error decreases as sample size increases (since \(SE\) shrinks) and increases as the desired confidence level increases (a higher critical value is needed for more confidence).

title: Estimation
text:
Confidence Level and Its Interpretation
Common confidence levels and their corresponding critical \(z\)-values (for large samples/known \(\sigma\)):



Confidence Level
\(\alpha\)
Critical \(z_{\alpha/2}\)




90%
0.10
1.645


95%
0.05
1.96


99%
0.01
2.576









Correct interpretation of a 95% CI: “If we were to repeat this study many times, drawing a new random sample each time and constructing a CI the same way, approximately 95% of those intervals would contain the true population parameter.” It is incorrect to say “there is a 95% probability that the true parameter lies in this particular interval”. Under the frequentist framework, the true parameter is a fixed (though unknown) constant, and any single computed interval either contains it or does not (this is closer to the Bayesian credible interval interpretation).

title: Estimation
section: Worked Example (Confidence interval for a mean)
text:
Worked Example (Confidence interval for a mean)
Using our earlier sample: \(n=36\) patients, \(\bar{x}=126\) mmHg, \(s=12\) mmHg. Construct a 95% CI for the true mean blood pressure.
Step 1: Compute the standard error: \(SE = s/\sqrt{n} = 12/\sqrt{36} = 2.0\).
Step 2: Find the critical value: for a 95% CI with \(n-1=35\) df
\(t_{0.025,35}\approx 2.03\) (close to the \(z\) value of 1.96 for large \(n\)).
Step 3: Compute the margin of error: \(ME = 2.03\times2.0=4.06\).
Step 4: Construct the interval: \[126 \pm 4.06 = (121.9,\ 130.1) \text{ mmHg}\]
Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean blood pressure of the population from which this sample was drawn lies between 121.9 and 130.1 mmHg. Note this interval includes 130 mmHg, the value tested in Section 9’s hypothesis test — consistent with that test’s borderline result (p = 0.046, just below 0.05, so technically still significant, illustrating that CIs and hypothesis tests can appear to be right at the boundary of agreement/disagreement when a result is only marginally significant).

title: Estimation
section: Determine the confidence interval around mean in R
text:
Determine the confidence interval around mean in R
We can use meanCI() from DescTools to calculate CI around mean in R.

# CI around mean for problem above
mean_sbp <- 126
sd_sbp <- 12
n <- 36

se <- sd_sbp / sqrt(n)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)

lower <- mean_sbp - t_crit * se
upper <- mean_sbp + t_crit * se

print(paste("Confidence interval around", mean_sbp, "is", c(lower, upper)))

#> [1] "Confidence interval around 126 is 121.939784143499"
#> [2] "Confidence interval around 126 is 130.060215856501"

# CI around mean for dataset
data <- readxl::read_excel("Section2/Categorical data analysis/Datasets/wcgs.xls")

#CI around mean  for data
DescTools::MeanCI(x = data$bmi, sd = sd(data$bmi), conf.level = 0.95,sides = "two.sided") 

#>     mean   lwr.ci   upr.ci 
#> 24.51837 24.42877 24.60798

title: Estimation
section: Worked Example: Confidence Interval for Proportion
text:
Worked Example: Confidence Interval for Proportion
In a survey of \(n=400\) adults, 92 report having been vaccinated against influenza this season. Construct a 95% CI for the true population proportion vaccinated.
Step 1: \(\hat{p} = 92/400 = 0.23\).
Step 2: \(SE(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.23(1-0.23)}{400}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.1771}{400}} = \sqrt{0.000443}=0.02104\)
Step 3: \(ME = 1.96\times0.02104=0.0412\)
Step 4: \[0.23 \pm 0.0412 = (0.189,\ 0.271) \text{ or } (18.9\%,\ 27.1\%)\]
Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true influenza vaccination rate in the population is between 18.9% and 27.1%.

title: Estimation
section: Determine the confidence interval around proportion in R
text:
Determine the confidence interval around proportion in R
Confidence intervals can be produced for either binomial or multinomial proportions.
The binom.test() function in the native stats package will provide the Clopper-Pearson confidence interval for a binomial proportion. Other methods for a binomial proportion are provided by the BinomCI() function in the DescTools package, as well as by various functions in the PropCIs package. Different methods available for calculating CI around binary variable include : "wilson", "wald", "agresti-coull", "jeffreys", "modified wilson", "modified jeffreys","clopper-pearson", "arcsine", "logit", "witting", "pratt"
Confidence intervals for multinomial proportions can be produced with the MultinomCI() function in the DescTools package.

# CI for proportion calculation manually for problem above
p <- 60 / 200
k <- p + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / 200)

print(paste("The confidence interval around proportion", p, "is", round(k[1],2), "and ", round(k[2],2) ))

#> [1] "The confidence interval around proportion 0.3 is 0.24 and  0.36"

# # CI for proportion calculation for dataset
data <- readxl::read_excel("Section2/Categorical data analysis/Datasets/wcgs.xls")

# Confidence interval for binary variable  
a<- addmargins(table(data$chd69))  
# In the above table No is 2897 and yes is 257 and total of 3154 

DescTools::BinomCI(x = a[2],n = a[3], method = "clopper")*100 # we can select different methods depending on need  

#>           est   lwr.ci   upr.ci
#> [1,] 8.148383 7.216913 9.158305

# Confidence interval around multinomial variable 
b<- addmargins(table(data$agec))  
# In the above table for each categories 35-40, 41-45, 46-50, 51-55 and 56-60, number of observations are 543, 1091, 750, 528, and 242 respectively

DescTools::MultinomCI( x = b, method = "goodman")*100 # we can select different methods depending on need

title: Estimation
text:
Confidence Interval vs. Prediction Interval








Feature
Confidence Interval
Prediction Interval




Estimates
A population parameter (e.g., the true mean \(\mu\))
A single future/individual observation


Width
Narrower
Always wider than the CI for the same data and confidence level


Accounts for
Uncertainty in estimating the parameter only
Uncertainty in estimating the parameter plus the natural variability of individual observations


Formula (mean)
\(\bar{x}\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\dfrac{s}{\sqrt n}\)
\(\bar{x}\pm t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\, s\sqrt{1+\dfrac{1}{n}}\)


Example question
“What is the plausible range for the average blood pressure of all patients like this?”
“What is the plausible range of blood pressure for one new patient?”









A useful way to remember the distinction: a confidence interval narrows toward zero width as \(n\to\infty\) (we can estimate the population mean with near-perfect precision given enough data), but a prediction interval never shrinks below the natural variability of individual observations (\(s\)), no matter how large \(n\) becomes, individual patients will always vary, even if we know the population mean exactly.

title: Estimation
text:
Summary

Point estimation provides a single best-guess value for a parameter; interval estimation adds a range reflecting the estimate’s precision.
The standard error measures the variability of the sample statistic itself (distinct from the SD, which measures variability of individual observations) and shrinks as \(n\) increases.
A confidence interval = point estimate ± (critical value × standard error); wider intervals reflect either smaller sample sizes or higher confidence levels.
The correct interpretation of a 95% CI concerns the long-run performance of the method, not the probability that a specific interval contains the true parameter.
A prediction interval is always wider than a confidence interval because it must account for individual-level variability in addition to parameter uncertainty.

title: Estimation
text: References

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Introduction
We have gone through descriptive statistics and probability distributions. Now its turn to inferential statistics. It is used to draw conclusions about a population from sample data. Hypothesis testing is a formal procedure for deciding whether sample data provide enough evidence to support a claim about a population.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Population Parameter vs. Sample Statistic
Population and the sample are two of the most fundamental concepts in statistics. A population parameter (e.g., \(\mu\), \(\sigma\), \(\pi\)) is a fixed, usually unknown, numerical characteristic of an entire population. A sample statistic (e.g., \(\bar{x}\), \(s\), \(\hat{p}\)) is computed from sample data and used to estimate the corresponding parameter. Hypothesis testing uses sample statistic, together with its known sampling distribution, to make a probabilistic statement about the population parameter.

title: Hypothesis Testing
section: Research Hypothesis, Null, and Alternative Hypothesis
text:
Research Hypothesis, Null, and Alternative Hypothesis

Research hypothesis: The substantive question or claim the investigator wants to evaluate (e.g., “a new anti-hypertensive drug lowers blood pressure more than the standard drug”).
Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): A statement of “no effect,” “no difference,” or “no association” .It is the default position that is assumed true until evidence suggests otherwise.
Example: \(H_0: \mu_{new}=\mu_{standard}\).
Alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\) or \(H_a\)): The statement that contradicts \(H_0\), representing what the researcher suspects may actually be true.
Example: \(H_a: \mu_{new} \ne \mu_{standard}\) (or \(<\), or \(>\), depending on the research question).







Hypothesis testing follows the logic of a courtroom trial: \(H_0\) (“the defendant is innocent”) is assumed true until the evidence (data) is strong enough to reject it “beyond reasonable doubt” (a pre-specified significance level) in favor of \(H_a\) (“the defendant is guilty”). We never “prove” \(H_0\) true; we only fail to reject it, or reject it in favor of \(H_a\).

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Significance Level (\(\alpha\))
The significance level, \(\alpha\), is the threshold probability of incorrectly rejecting a true null hypothesis (a Type I Error ) that the researcher is willing to accept, chosen before collecting/analyzing data. Common conventions: \(\alpha=0.05\) (5%), \(\alpha=0.01\) (1%).

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Test Statistic
A test statistic is a single value, computed from the sample data, that measures how far the observed data deviate from what would be expected under \(H_0\). Its form depends on the hypothesis and data type (e.g., \(z\), \(t\), \(\chi^2\), \(F\) ).
General structure of test statistics is as follows: \[\text{Test statistic} = \frac{\text{Observed estimate} - \text{Hypothesized value under } H_0}{\text{Standard error of the estimate}}\]

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
P-value
The p-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic as extreme as, or more extreme than, the one observed, assuming \(H_0\) is true. A small p-value indicates the observed data would be unusual if \(H_0\) were true, providing evidence against \(H_0\).






A p-value is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true, and it is not the probability the results occurred “by chance” in a broad sense. It is a conditional probability: \(P(\text{data this extreme or more} \mid H_0 \text{ true})\). Misinterpreting the p-value is one of the most common errors in the interpretation of statistical results.









P values are among the most widely used, and widely misused, tools in cancer research, and understanding their common pitfalls is essential for sound statistical interpretation.
One frequent error is overemphasizing statistical significance at the expense of clinical significance. In large datasets such as cancer registries or EHRs, even trivially small effects can yield small P values, so researchers should always report effect size estimates alongside confidence intervals and ask whether the magnitude of effect is clinically meaningful, not just statistically detectable. Related to this is the problem of applying mis-specified models or inappropriate testing procedures, for example using parametric tests on small animal-study samples without first checking normality assumptions. This can be addressed by verifying distributional assumptions beforehand or defaulting to more robust nonparametric alternatives.
Another major concern is inflated Type I error from multiple comparisons, a particular risk when screening large numbers of variables, such as testing associations between thousands of gene expression levels and survival outcomes in TCGA data. Controlling the false discovery rate or applying familywise error corrections helps guard against spurious findings. Equally common is the misinterpretation of a non-significant result (P > 0.05) as evidence of “no difference,” for instance wrongly concluding two cancer treatments are equally effective, when in fact failure to reject the null does not establish equivalence. Equivalence, non-inferiority, or superiority testing frameworks are better suited to answering that specific question.
Finally, P values derived from observational data carry their own risks. A significant result in cancer registry analysis may simply reflect unaddressed confounding rather than a true causal association. Because observational designs lack randomization, appropriate adjustment methods (multivariable modeling, propensity scores, or other confounder-control techniques) are necessary before a P value can be interpreted as meaningful evidence. Together, these examples underscore a broader lesson: P values should be interpreted alongside effect sizes, study design, and appropriate methodological safeguards rather than treated as a stand-alone verdict on scientific truth(Wang and Long 2022).

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Critical Value and Decision Rule
The critical value is the cutoff value of the test statistic that separates the “rejection region” from the “non-rejection region,” determined by \(\alpha\) and the sampling distribution of the test statistic.
Decision for a hypothesis can be taken using two approaches. First decision rule is based on p-value (p-value approach). In this approach, null hypothesis (\(H_0\)) is rejected if p-value \(\le \alpha\), and otherwise failed to reject null hypothesis (\(H_0\)). Second decison rule is based on critical value (critical value approach). In this appraoch, \(H_0\) is rejected if the test statistic falls in the rejection region (beyond the critical value), and otherwise, fail to reject \(H_0\).
Both approaches always give the same conclusion for a given \(\alpha\).


Worked Example
A researcher tests whether a new drug changes mean blood pressure from the population mean of \(\mu_0=130\) mmHg. A sample of \(n=36\) patients gives \(\bar{x}=126\) mmHg, \(s=12\) mmHg. Test at \(\alpha=0.05\) (two-tailed).
Step 1: State hypotheses: \(H_0: \mu=130\) vs. \(H_a: \mu\ne130\).
Step 2: Level of significance (\(\alpha=0.05\))
Step 3: Compute the test statistic (using \(z\) since \(n\) is reasonably large)
\[ SE = s/\sqrt{n} = 12/\sqrt{36}=12/6=2.0 \] \[z = \frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{SE} = \frac{126-130}{2.0} = -2.0\]
Step 4: Determine P-value or critical value

Find the p-value for a two-tailed test:

\(p = 2\times P(Z\le-2.0) = 2\times0.0228=0.0456\).

Critical value of Z at α=0.05 is -1.96 (from Z table)

Step 5: Decision and conclusion: When p-value is compared with \(\alpha=0.05\) or critical value is compared with test statistics. Since \(0.0456<0.05\) or -2.0 is less than -1.96, \(H_0\) is rejected. Thus,there is statistically significant evidence, at the 5% level, that mean blood pressure differs from 130 mmHg.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Statistical Significance vs. Practical (Clinical) Significance
Statistical significance means the observed effect is unlikely to have arisen from chance alone (p ≤ α), given the sample size and variability. Practical (or clinical) significance asks whether the size of the effect is large enough to matter in real-world, clinical, or public health terms.






With a very large sample size, even a tiny, clinically meaningless difference (e.g., a 0.5 mmHg drop in blood pressure) can be statistically significant. Conversely, with a small sample, a large, clinically important effect may fail to reach statistical significance. Always report and interpret effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside p-values, not p-values alone.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
One-Tailed vs. Two-Tailed Tests

Two-tailed test: Tests for a difference in either direction (\(H_a: \mu \ne \mu_0\)). The rejection region is split between both tails of the distribution.
One-tailed test: Tests for a difference in one specific direction only (\(H_a: \mu>\mu_0\) or \(H_a:\mu<\mu_0\)). The entire rejection region is in one tail. It can be right tailed and left tailed



Figure: Right-tailed hypothesis test





Figure: Left-tailed hypothesis test



Choosing a tail: A one-tailed test should be specified before looking at the data and only when there is a strong a priori reason to test in only one direction (e.g., testing whether a new drug is better than placebo, not just different). Two-tailed tests are more conservative and are the standard default in most biomedical research.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
The Decision Matrix









\(H_0\) is actually True
\(H_0\) is actually False




Reject \(H_0\)
Type I Error (probability = \(\alpha\))
Correct decision (power = \(1-\beta\))


Fail to reject \(H_0\)
Correct decision (probability = \(1-\alpha\))
Type II Error (probability = \(\beta\))

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Type I Error






Type I error occurs when we reject a true null hypothesis, concluding that there is an effect/difference when, in reality, there is none. This is a “false positive” finding. Its probability is exactly \(\alpha\), the significance level chosen by the researcher.



Clinical example: Concluding that a new drug lowers blood pressure more effectively than the standard treatment, when in truth the two treatments are equally effective leading to unnecessary adoption of a more expensive or riskier drug with no real benefit.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Type II Error






Type II error occurs when we fail to reject a false null hypothesis concluding that there is no effect/difference when, in reality, one exists. This is a “false negative” finding. Its probability is denoted \(\beta\).



Clinical example: Concluding that a new drug is no more effective than the standard treatment, when it actually is effective leading to a genuinely beneficial treatment being abandoned or never adopted.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Statistical Power
Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. It is correctly detecting a real effect when one truly exists: \[\text{Power} = 1-\beta\]
Power is influenced by four main factors:

Sample size (\(n\)): Larger samples increase power (more precise estimates, smaller standard errors).
Effect size: Larger true differences between groups are easier to detect, increasing power.
Significance level (\(\alpha\)): A larger \(\alpha\) (e.g., 0.10 instead of 0.05) increases power but also increases the Type I error rate. There is a direct trade-off between power and Type-I error.
Variability in the data (\(\sigma\)): Less variability (noise) increases power.

Conventionally, studies are designed to achieve power \(\ge 80\%\) (i.e., \(\beta \le 0.20\)), meaning there is at least an 80% chance of detecting a true effect of the specified size if it exists. These parameters are used to calculate sample size during study design and before data collection.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Confidence Level
The confidence level (\(1-\alpha\)) is the complement of the Type I error rate, and represents the long-run proportion of confidence intervals (constructed the same way, from repeated samples) that would contain the true population parameter. A 95% confidence level corresponds to \(\alpha=0.05\). Confidence intervals are covered in depth later in this chapter Interval Estimation and the Confidence Interval.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Relationship Among \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), and Power



Fig. Relationship between alpha error , beta error and power








There is an inherent trade-off between \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) for a fixed sample size: reducing the Type I error rate (using a smaller \(\alpha\), e.g., 0.01 instead of 0.05) makes it harder to reject \(H_0\), which increases the Type II error rate (\(\beta\)) and decreases power, unless sample size is also increased to compensate. Increasing sample size is the primary way to reduce \(\beta\) (increase power) without increasing \(\alpha\).

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Example (Illustrating the Trade-off)
A clinical trial is designed to detect a 5 mmHg reduction in blood pressure. With \(n=30\) per group, the study has 60% power at \(\alpha=0.05\), meaning there is a 40% chance (\(\beta=0.40\)) of missing a true 5 mmHg effect (a Type II error) if it exists. To increase power to the conventional 80% threshold while keeping \(\alpha=0.05\) fixed, the researcher must increase the sample size (e.g., to \(n=64\) per group, calculated using standard power-analysis formulas), sample size calculation is covered in a dedicated chapter later in this book ?sec-ssc_and_power.

title: Hypothesis Testing
section: Diagram: Overlapping Sampling Distributions Under \(H_0\) and \(H_a\)
text:
Diagram: Overlapping Sampling Distributions Under \(H_0\) and \(H_a\)

The critical value that defines \(\alpha\) under \(H_0\) simultaneously defines \(\beta\) under \(H_a\) , the two error rates are linked through the same decision threshold, which is why changing \(\alpha\) mechanically changes \(\beta\) (for fixed \(n\) and effect size).

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Summary

Hypothesis testing formally evaluates whether sample data provide sufficient evidence against \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a\).
The significance level \(\alpha\) sets the tolerance for Type I error; the p-value quantifies the evidence against \(H_0\).
Reject \(H_0\) when p-value \(\le\alpha\), or equivalently when the test statistic exceeds the critical value.
Statistical significance is not the same as clinical significance.
Two-tailed tests are the standard default. One-tailed tests require strong prior justification.

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
References

title: Association Between Two Numeric Variables
crumbs: 17  Association Between Two Numeric Variables

title: Association Between Two Numeric Variables
text:
Assumptions

Both \(X\) and \(Y\) are continuous (interval/ratio) numeric variables.
The relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\) is (approximately) linear.
For inference (hypothesis tests / CIs), the pairs \((X,Y)\) come from a bivariate normal distribution — in practice this is usually checked by inspecting the marginal distributions of \(X\) and \(Y\) for gross non-normality and skew.
Observations are independent of one another.
No excessively influential outliers.
Variance of \(Y\) is reasonably constant across the range of \(X\) (homoscedasticity).
crumbs: 17  Association Between Two Numeric Variables

title: Association Between Two Numeric Variables
text:
Properties

\(-1 \le r \le 1\); \(r=1\) is perfect positive linear association, \(r=-1\) perfect negative linear association, \(r=0\) no linear association.
\(r\) is unit-free (dimensionless) and symmetric: \(r_{xy} = r_{yx}\).
\(r\) measures only linear association — a strong curved relationship can produce a small \(r\).
\(r\) is sensitive to outliers and to restriction of range.
\(r^2\) (the coefficient of determination) is the proportion of variance in \(Y\) “explained” by the linear relationship with \(X\).
Correlation does not imply causation.
crumbs: 17  Association Between Two Numeric Variables

title: Association Between Two Numeric Variables
text:
A rule-of-thumb interpretation scale



\(|r|\)
Strength of linear association




0.00 – 0.09
Negligible


0.10 – 0.39
Weak


0.40 – 0.69
Moderate


0.70 – 0.89
Strong


0.90 – 1.00
Very strong



These cut-points (adapted from conventions such as Cohen, 1988) are a rough guide only; the meaningfulness of a given \(r\) always depends on the substantive context.

title: Association Between Two Numeric Variables
text:
Hypothesis test for \(\rho\)
To test \(H_0: \rho = 0\) versus \(H_1: \rho \ne 0\):
\[
t = r\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}} \qquad \sim \; t_{(n-2)} \text{ under } H_0
\tag{18.3}\]
crumbs: 17  Association Between Two Numeric Variables

title: Association Between Two Numeric Variables
text:
Confidence interval for \(\rho\) (Fisher’s \(z\)-transformation)
Because the sampling distribution of \(r\) is skewed (except when \(\rho=0\)), Fisher’s \(z\)-transformation is used:
\[
z' = \tfrac12 \ln\!\left(\frac{1+r}{1-r}\right), \qquad SE(z') = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n-3}}
\]
A \(95\%\) CI for \(z'\) is \(z' \pm 1.96 \times SE(z')\); each limit is back-transformed with
\[
r = \frac{e^{2z'}-1}{e^{2z'}+1}
\]

text:
Step 2: Apply the deviation formula
\[
\bar x = \frac{694}{10}=69.4 \qquad \bar y=\frac{1750}{10}=175.0
\]
\[
r=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)}{\sqrt{\sum(x-\bar x)^2 \sum(y-\bar y)^2}}
=\frac{831.0}{\sqrt{72.4 \times 16624}}
=\frac{831.0}{\sqrt{1{,}203{,}977.6}}
=\frac{831.0}{1097.26}
\]

r_manual <- sum(tab$dx_dy) / sqrt(sum(tab$dx2) * sum(tab$dy2))
r_manual

#> [1] 0.7574675


By hand, \(r = 0.757\) — a strong, positive linear association between height and weight in this subsample.

Cross-check with the computational (raw-score) formula

Sx <- sum(x); Sy <- sum(y); Sxy <- sum(x*y); Sx2 <- sum(x^2); Sy2 <- sum(y^2)
r_raw <- (n*Sxy - Sx*Sy) / sqrt((n*Sx2 - Sx^2) * (n*Sy2 - Sy^2))
data.frame(Sx, Sy, Sxy, Sx2, Sy2, r_raw)

#>    Sx   Sy    Sxy   Sx2    Sy2     r_raw
#> 1 694 1750 122281 48236 322874 0.7574675


Both formulas agree exactly, as they must algebraically.
crumbs: 17  Association Between Two Numeric Variables

title: Association Between Two Numeric Variables
text:
Step 3: Test \(H_0: \rho = 0\)
\[
t = r\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}} = 0.757\sqrt{\frac{8}{1-0.757^2}}
\]

t_manual  <- r_manual * sqrt((n - 2) / (1 - r_manual^2))
df_manual <- n - 2
p_manual  <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_manual), df = df_manual)
data.frame(t = t_manual, df = df_manual, p_value = p_manual)

#>         t df    p_value
#> 1 3.28156  8 0.01116178


With \(t = 3.28\) on \(8\) df, \(p = 0.011\): we reject \(H_0\) at the \(5\%\) level and conclude there is a statistically significant positive linear association between height and weight in this small sample.

The hand-calculated \(r\), \(t\), \(df\), and \(p\)-value match R’s cor.test() output exactly — confirming the manual arithmetic.

title: Association Between Two Numeric Variables
section: When to use Spearman instead of Pearson
text:
When to use Spearman instead of Pearson
Spearman’s coefficient should be preferred over Pearson’s when:

The variables are ordinal rather than truly numeric (e.g., pain scores, tumour grade).
The data are numeric but markedly non-normal or skewed (Pearson’s inferential validity is weakened).
There are influential outliers that would distort \(r\).
The relationship is monotonic but not linear (consistently increasing or decreasing, but curved) — Spearman still detects this fully, whereas Pearson under-estimates it.
crumbs: 17  Association Between Two Numeric Variables

title: Association Between Two Numeric Variables
text:
Definition
Spearman’s rank correlation is simply the Pearson correlation coefficient computed on the ranks of \(X\) and \(Y\) rather than on their raw values. If there are no tied ranks, this simplifies to the well-known shortcut formula:
\[
r_s = 1-\frac{6\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^2}{n(n^2-1)}, \qquad d_i = \operatorname{rank}(x_i)-\operatorname{rank}(y_i)
\tag{20.1}\]
Tied values are given the average of the ranks they would otherwise occupy. When ties are present, Equation 20.1 is only an approximation; the exact value is obtained by computing the ordinary Pearson formula (Equation 18.1) on the rank-transformed data. Software (including R) uses this ties-corrected version by default.
crumbs: 17  Association Between Two Numeric Variables

title: Association Between Two Numeric Variables
text:
Assumptions and properties

Requires only that the data be at least ordinal, and that the relationship be monotonic.
\(-1 \le r_s \le 1\), same interpretation of sign and magnitude as Pearson’s \(r\), but describing a monotonic rather than strictly linear trend.
Far more robust to outliers than Pearson’s \(r\), because extreme values are pulled in by ranking.
Hypothesis test of \(H_0: \rho_s = 0\) can use the same \(t\)-approximation as Pearson’s (Equation 18.3), substituting \(r_s\) for \(r\), for moderate/large \(n\); exact permutation-based \(p\)-values are used for small \(n\) without ties.

text:
Step 5: Spearman correlation

cor.test(wcgs$chol, wcgs$sbp, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)

#> 
#>  Spearman's rank correlation rho
#> 
#> data:  wcgs$chol and wcgs$sbp
#> S = 4457547658, p-value = 8.779e-15
#> alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
#> sample estimates:
#>       rho 
#> 0.1377588


Interpretation: \(r_s = 0.138\), \(p < 0.001\). Because \(n\) is large, even this weak monotonic association is statistically significant — a reminder that with large samples, statistical significance and practical/clinical importance are not the same thing. Note exact = FALSE is required here because chol contains tied values and is large, so R falls back on the asymptotic \(t\)-approximation for the \(p\)-value.

cor.test(wcgs$height, wcgs$weight, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)

#> 
#>  Spearman's rank correlation rho
#> 
#> data:  wcgs$height and wcgs$weight
#> S = 2409320566, p-value < 2.2e-16
#> alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
#> sample estimates:
#>       rho 
#> 0.5392548


For height and weight, Pearson (\(r=0.533\)) and Spearman (\(r_s=0.529\)) agree closely — expected, since this relationship is close to linear and both variables are reasonably symmetric.

title: Categorical data analysis
text:
Types of Categorical Data
This chapter reviews the core tools for analyzing categorical data using proportions, chi-square and Fisher’s exact tests, McNemar’s test for paired data, risk ratios and odds ratios, screening test characteristics, and stratified (Mantel-Haenszel) analysis. These methods answer the same substantive question that logistic regression answers later in this chapter — whether an outcome is associated with an exposure, and how strong that association is — but do so without fitting a model, and several of them (the odds ratio, the chi-square test, stratified analysis) reappear directly inside logistic regression once covariates are added. Examples below use the Western Collaborative Group Study (wcgs) data already introduced in this chapter, with ten-year coronary heart disease status (chd69) as the outcome.
Categorical variables come in three forms, and knowing which one you have determines which test applies:
Two probability distributions underlie most of the methods in this section. The binomial distribution describes the number of “successes” in n independent trials with a constant probability of success, and applies whenever the outcome is binary. The multinomial distribution extends this to outcomes with more than two categories. Nearly every method below — proportions, chi-square tests, risk ratios, odds ratios — is a way of comparing observed binomial or multinomial counts to what would be expected under a null hypothesis.

title: Categorical data analysis
text:
Binary: exactly two categories (e.g., chd69: Yes/No)
Nominal: more than two categories with no inherent order (e.g., blood type, behpat)
Ordinal: more than two categories with a meaningful order but unequal or unknown spacing between them (e.g., pain severity: none/mild/moderate/severe)

title: Categorical data analysis
text:
Inference for a Single Proportion
For a binary outcome observed in a sample of size \(n\) with \(x\) successes, the sample proportion is \(\hat{p}=x/n\). When both \(n\hat p\) and \(n(1-\hat p)\) exceed 5, \(\hat p\) is approximately normal, which justifies the Wald test and confidence interval:
\[ Z_{stat}=\frac{\hat{p}-\pi_0}{\sqrt{\pi_0(1-\pi_0)/n}} \qquad \hat{p} \pm Z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}} \]
When the sample is small, or \(\hat p\) is close to 0 or 1, the Wald interval is known to under-cover; the exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval or the Agresti-Coull interval (Agresti & Coull, 1998, The American Statistician, 52, 119-126) are preferred in that setting.

# Overall proportion of CHD in the wcgs cohort
table(data$chd69)

#> 
#>   No  Yes 
#> 2897  257

x <- sum(data$chd69 == "Yes")
n <- nrow(data)

# One-sample test: is the CHD rate different from 10%?
prop.test(x, n, p = 0.10, correct = FALSE)

#> 
#>  1-sample proportions test without continuity correction
#> 
#> data:  x out of n, null probability 0.1
#> X-squared = 12.015, df = 1, p-value = 0.0005278
#> alternative hypothesis: true p is not equal to 0.1
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.07243754 0.09154836
#> sample estimates:
#>          p 
#> 0.08148383

# Exact binomial test and confidence interval
binom.test(x, n, p = 0.10)

#> 
#>  Exact binomial test
#> 
#> data:  x and n
#> number of successes = 257, number of trials = 3154, p-value = 0.0004093
#> alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.1
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.07216913 0.09158305
#> sample estimates:
#> probability of success 
#>             0.08148383



Interpretation
Of the 3,154 participants, 257 developed CHD, giving \(\hat p = 0.081\) (95% Wald CI: 7.2%, 9.1%). Testing against \(\pi_0 = 0.10\) gives Z = -3.47, p = 0.0005, so the CHD rate in this cohort is significantly lower than 10%.
For small subgroups the choice of interval matters more. Restricting to the youngest age category (agec == "35-40", n = 543, 31 events, \(\hat p = 0.057\)), the Wald interval (3.8%, 7.7%) sits slightly lower than the exact interval (3.9%, 8.0%) — a reminder that the Wald method is not the recommended choice once \(n\) or \(\hat p\) is small.

young <- data |> dplyr::filter(agec == "35-40")
x2 <- sum(young$chd69 == "Yes"); n2 <- nrow(young)
phat <- x2 / n2

# Wald interval
phat + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n2)

#> [1] 0.03757508 0.07660540

# Exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval
binom.test(x2, n2)$conf.int

#> [1] 0.03911595 0.08005924
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95

title: Categorical data analysis
text:
Comparing Two Independent Proportions
To compare proportions between two independent groups, the Wald test statistic and confidence interval are:
\[ Z_{stat}=\frac{(\hat p_1-\hat p_2)-\delta_0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)}{n_2}}} \qquad (\hat p_1-\hat p_2)\pm Z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)}{n_1}+\frac{\hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)}{n_2}} \]

tab_sc <- table(data$smoke, data$chd69)[c("Yes","No"), c("Yes","No")]
tab_sc  # rows = smoker, columns = chd69

#>      
#>        Yes   No
#>   Yes  159 1343
#>   No    98 1554

prop.test(tab_sc, correct = FALSE)

#> 
#>  2-sample test for equality of proportions without continuity correction
#> 
#> data:  tab_sc
#> X-squared = 22.764, df = 1, p-value = 1.831e-06
#> alternative hypothesis: two.sided
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  0.02725364 0.06582000
#> sample estimates:
#>     prop 1     prop 2 
#> 0.10585885 0.05932203



Interpretation
The CHD rate is 10.6% among smokers versus 5.9% among non-smokers, a difference of 4.7 percentage points (95% CI: 2.7, 6.6). The test statistic (Z ≈ 4.8, equivalent to the χ² statistic below) gives p < 0.0001, so smokers have a significantly higher CHD rate than non-smokers in this cohort.

title: Categorical data analysis
text:
McNemar’s Test for Matched Pairs
The tests above assume independent samples. When the same subjects are measured twice (before/after, matched pairs, two raters), the two proportions are correlated and the ordinary two-proportion test no longer applies. McNemar’s test instead uses only the discordant pairs — the cases where the two measurements disagree:
\[ \chi^2_{stat}=\frac{(b-c)^2}{b+c}, \quad df=1 \]
where \(b\) and \(c\) are the two off-diagonal (discordant) cell counts of the \(2\times2\) paired table.

# Illustrative matched-pairs example: outcome (improved/not) under two paired treatments
pairs_tab <- matrix(c(2, 2, 6, 6), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                     dimnames = list("Treatment B" = c("Improved", "Not improved"),
                                      "Treatment A" = c("Improved", "Not improved")))
pairs_tab

#>               Treatment A
#> Treatment B    Improved Not improved
#>   Improved            2            2
#>   Not improved        6            6

mcnemar.test(pairs_tab, correct = FALSE)   # matches the hand formula above

#> 
#>  McNemar's Chi-squared test
#> 
#> data:  pairs_tab
#> McNemar's chi-squared = 2, df = 1, p-value = 0.1573

mcnemar.test(pairs_tab)                    # default applies Yates' continuity correction

#> 
#>  McNemar's Chi-squared test with continuity correction
#> 
#> data:  pairs_tab
#> McNemar's chi-squared = 1.125, df = 1, p-value = 0.2888



Interpretation
Here \(\chi^2=(2-6)^2/(2+6)=2\), df = 1, p = 0.157. There is not enough evidence that the two treatments differ in their probability of improvement.

title: Categorical data analysis
text:
Chi-Square Test of Independence
For two independent categorical variables laid out in an \(r\times c\) contingency table, the chi-square test compares observed to expected cell counts under independence:
\[ \chi^2_{stat}=\sum_{\text{all cells}}\frac{(f_o-f_e)^2}{f_e}, \qquad f_e=\frac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{n}, \qquad df=(r-1)(c-1) \]
The approximation is reliable when at least 80% of expected cell counts are \(\ge5\) and none is below 1; otherwise use Fisher’s exact test.

chisq.test(tab_sc, correct = FALSE)              # standard chi-square test

#> 
#>  Pearson's Chi-squared test
#> 
#> data:  tab_sc
#> X-squared = 22.764, df = 1, p-value = 1.831e-06

chisq.test(tab_sc, correct = FALSE)$expected      # check the >=5 rule

#>      
#>            Yes       No
#>   Yes 122.3887 1379.611
#>   No  134.6113 1517.389

chisq.test(tab_sc, correct = TRUE)               # Yates' continuity correction

#> 
#>  Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction
#> 
#> data:  tab_sc
#> X-squared = 22.147, df = 1, p-value = 2.526e-06

# Extending to an r x c table: behavior pattern (4 levels) by CHD status
table(data$behpat, data$chd69)

#>     
#>        No  Yes
#>   A1  234   30
#>   A2 1177  148
#>   B3 1155   61
#>   B4  331   18

chisq.test(table(data$behpat, data$chd69))

#> 
#>  Pearson's Chi-squared test
#> 
#> data:  table(data$behpat, data$chd69)
#> X-squared = 39.916, df = 3, p-value = 1.11e-08



Interpretation
For smoking status by CHD, \(\chi^2=22.76\), df = 1, p < 0.0001 (Yates-corrected: \(\chi^2=22.15\), p < 0.0001) — smoking status and CHD are not independent. The behpat-by-chd69 table extends the same logic to a \(4\times2\) table without changing the test statistic or its interpretation, only the degrees of freedom.

title: Categorical data analysis
text:
Fisher’s Exact Test
When one or more expected cell counts fall below 5, the chi-square approximation is unreliable. Fisher’s exact test instead conditions on the observed row and column totals and computes the exact probability of the observed table (and all more extreme tables) from the hypergeometric distribution:
\[ p(a)=\frac{\binom{a+b}{a}\binom{c+d}{c}}{\binom{n}{a+c}} \]
Unlike the chi-square test, Fisher’s exact test has no test statistic or critical value — only a p-value — and it remains valid even with very small samples, zero cells, or highly unbalanced tables.

fisher.test(tab_sc)

#> 
#>  Fisher's Exact Test for Count Data
#> 
#> data:  tab_sc
#> p-value = 2.366e-06
#> alternative hypothesis: true odds ratio is not equal to 1
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  1.434194 2.466073
#> sample estimates:
#> odds ratio 
#>   1.876954



Interpretation
Fisher’s exact test gives p < 0.0001 for the smoking/CHD table, agreeing with the chi-square result above (expected counts here are all well above 5, so either test is valid; Fisher’s test is shown for comparison, and it is the correct choice whenever that condition fails).

title: Categorical data analysis
text:
Risk Ratio and Odds Ratio
For a \(2\times2\) table of exposure by disease,




Disease +
Disease −




Exposed
a
b


Unexposed
c
d



the risk ratio compares the probability of disease between exposed and unexposed groups, and the odds ratio compares the odds:
\[ \hat{RR}=\frac{a/(a+b)}{c/(c+d)} \qquad \hat{OR}=\frac{ad}{bc} \]
Both are tested and estimated on the log scale, since \(\ln(\hat{RR})\) and \(\ln(\hat{OR})\) are approximately normal:
\[ SE[\ln(\hat{RR})]=\sqrt{\frac1a-\frac1{a+b}+\frac1c-\frac1{c+d}} \qquad SE[\ln(\hat{OR})]=\sqrt{\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c+\frac1d} \]

a  <- tab_sc["Yes","Yes"]; b <- tab_sc["Yes","No"]
c_ <- tab_sc["No","Yes"];  d <- tab_sc["No","No"]

# Risk ratio and 95% CI
RR <- (a/(a+b)) / (c_/(c_+d))
se_lnRR <- sqrt(1/a - 1/(a+b) + 1/c_ - 1/(c_+d))
c(RR = RR, exp(log(RR) + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se_lnRR))

#>       RR                   
#> 1.784478 1.401165 2.272653

# Odds ratio and 95% CI
OR <- (a*d) / (b*c_)
se_lnOR <- sqrt(1/a + 1/b + 1/c_ + 1/d)
c(OR = OR, exp(log(OR) + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se_lnOR))

#>       OR                   
#> 1.877353 1.444508 2.439901








The odds ratio and risk ratio answer slightly different questions and are not interchangeable, although they converge when the outcome is rare (here CHD is uncommon enough — about 8% — that RR = 1.78 and OR = 1.88 are close). The odds ratio is the quantity produced directly by logistic regression coefficients after exponentiating, which is why it, rather than the risk ratio, carries over into the regression models later in this chapter.




Interpretation
Smokers have 1.78 times the risk of developing CHD compared to non-smokers (95% CI: 1.40, 2.27), and 1.88 times the odds (95% CI: 1.44, 2.44). Both intervals exclude 1, confirming the association already identified by the chi-square and Fisher’s exact tests.

title: Categorical data analysis
text:
Screening Test Characteristics
Diagnostic and screening tests are evaluated against a \(2\times2\) table of test result by true disease status:




Disease +
Disease −




Test +
True Positive (TP)
False Positive (FP)


Test −
False Negative (FN)
True Negative (TN)



\[ Se=P(+|D)=\frac{TP}{TP+FN} \qquad Sp=P(-|\bar D)=\frac{TN}{TN+FP} \] \[ PPV=P(D|+)=\frac{TP}{TP+FP} \qquad NPV=P(\bar D|-)=\frac{TN}{TN+FN} \]
Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test itself and do not depend on how common the disease is. PPV and NPV, by contrast, depend heavily on disease prevalence — the same test performs very differently (in PPV terms) in a high-prevalence versus a low-prevalence population — and PPV/NPV cannot be validly calculated from a case-control sample where disease prevalence was fixed by the study design rather than observed.

screen <- matrix(c(180, 16, 20, 184), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(Test = c("Positive", "Negative"),
                                   Disease = c("Yes", "No")))
screen

#>           Disease
#> Test       Yes  No
#>   Positive 180  16
#>   Negative  20 184

sensitivity <- screen["Positive","Yes"] / sum(screen[,"Yes"])
specificity <- screen["Negative","No"]  / sum(screen[,"No"])
ppv <- screen["Positive","Yes"] / sum(screen["Positive",])
npv <- screen["Negative","No"]  / sum(screen["Negative",])
round(c(Sensitivity = sensitivity, Specificity = specificity, PPV = ppv, NPV = npv), 3)

#> Sensitivity Specificity         PPV         NPV 
#>       0.900       0.920       0.918       0.902



Interpretation
This hypothetical test has 90% sensitivity and 92% specificity, both comfortably above the commonly cited 80% threshold for a “good” screening test. In this sample (50% disease prevalence by design), PPV is 92% and NPV is 90%; in a lower-prevalence population, the same test’s PPV would be lower even though sensitivity and specificity stay the same.

title: Categorical data analysis
section: Stratified 2×2 Tables and the Mantel-Haenszel Method
text:
Stratified 2×2 Tables and the Mantel-Haenszel Method
A crude (unstratified) odds ratio, like the one computed above for smoking and CHD, can be confounded by a third variable that is associated with both the exposure and the outcome. The Mantel-Haenszel approach addresses this by splitting the data into strata of a potential confounder, testing for association within each stratum, and then pooling the stratum-specific evidence into a single adjusted test and effect estimate.
The Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test statistic, summed across \(q\) strata, is:
\[ Q_{MH}=\frac{\left[\sum_{h=1}^{q}(n_{h11}-m_{h11})\right]^2}{\sum_{h=1}^{q}v_{h11}}, \qquad m_{h11}=\frac{n_{h1.}n_{h.1}}{n_h}, \qquad v_{h11}=\frac{n_{h1.}n_{h2.}n_{h.1}n_{h.2}}{n_h^2(n_h-1)} \]
and the Mantel-Haenszel estimate of a common odds ratio across strata is:
\[ \hat\theta_{MH}=\frac{\sum_{h=1}^{q} n_{h11}n_{h22}/n_h}{\sum_{h=1}^{q} n_{h12}n_{h21}/n_h} \]
Here we stratify the smoking/CHD association by behavior pattern (dibpat: Type A vs. Type B), a variable known in this cohort to be associated with both smoking and CHD risk.

strat_tab <- xtabs(~ smoke + chd69 + dibpat, data = data)
strat_tab

#> , , dibpat = Type A
#> 
#>      chd69
#> smoke  No Yes
#>   No  714  70
#>   Yes 697 108
#> 
#> , , dibpat = Type B
#> 
#>      chd69
#> smoke  No Yes
#>   No  840  28
#>   Yes 646  51

# Stratum-specific odds ratios
apply(strat_tab, 3, function(t) (t[1,1]*t[2,2]) / (t[1,2]*t[2,1]))

#>   Type A   Type B 
#> 1.580488 2.368421

# Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test and common odds ratio
mantelhaen.test(strat_tab, correct = FALSE)

#> 
#>  Mantel-Haenszel chi-squared test without continuity correction
#> 
#> data:  strat_tab
#> Mantel-Haenszel X-squared = 19.486, df = 1, p-value = 1.013e-05
#> alternative hypothesis: true common odds ratio is not equal to 1
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>  1.380054 2.337230
#> sample estimates:
#> common odds ratio 
#>          1.795969



Test of Homogeneity (Breslow-Day Test)
Before pooling stratum-specific odds ratios into a single MH estimate, it is important to check that the strata actually share a common odds ratio (i.e., that behavior pattern is a confounder rather than an effect modifier). The Breslow-Day test evaluates \(H_0:\theta_1=\theta_2=\dots=\theta_q\) against a \(\chi^2_{q-1}\) distribution.

DescTools::BreslowDayTest(strat_tab)

#> 
#>  Breslow-Day test on Homogeneity of Odds Ratios
#> 
#> data:  strat_tab
#> X-squared = 1.9456, df = 1, p-value = 0.1631




Interpretation
The stratum-specific odds ratios (Type A: 1.58; Type B: 2.37) differ numerically, but the Breslow-Day test does not find this difference statistically significant (\(\chi^2\approx1.9\), p = 0.16), so it is reasonable to pool them. The CMH test rejects independence after adjusting for behavior pattern (\(Q_{MH}\approx19.5\), p < 0.0001), and the Mantel-Haenszel common odds ratio is about 1.80 — close to the crude, unadjusted odds ratio of 1.88 computed earlier, indicating that behavior pattern is not a strong confounder of the smoking-CHD association in this cohort. Had the stratum-specific and crude odds ratios diverged sharply, that would signal confounding requiring an adjusted (or model-based) estimate rather than the crude one.


Simpson’s Paradox
Stratified analysis exists because an association observed in aggregated data can behave very differently — even reverse direction — once a confounder is taken into account. A classic illustration comes from a comparison of two kidney stone treatments (Charig et al., 1986, BMJ):

kidney <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Stratum,       ~Treatment, ~Success, ~Failure,
  "Small stones", "A",         81,        6,
  "Small stones", "B",        234,       36,
  "Large stones", "A",        192,       71,
  "Large stones", "B",         55,       25,
  "Overall",       "A",       273,       77,
  "Overall",       "B",       289,       61
)
kidney |> dplyr::mutate(Success_rate = round(Success / (Success + Failure), 3))

#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   Stratum      Treatment Success Failure Success_rate
#>   <chr>        <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1 Small stones A              81       6        0.931
#> 2 Small stones B             234      36        0.867
#> 3 Large stones A             192      71        0.73 
#> 4 Large stones B              55      25        0.688
#> 5 Overall      A             273      77        0.78 
#> 6 Overall      B             289      61        0.826


Treatment A has the higher success rate for both small stones (93% vs. 87%) and large stones (73% vs. 69%) individually, yet Treatment B has the higher success rate overall (83% vs. 78%). The reversal happens because stone size is a confounder: Treatment A was used disproportionately on harder-to-treat large stones, while Treatment B was used mostly on easier small stones, which drags the unadjusted success rate for B upward. This is exactly the scenario the CMH test and Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio are designed to guard against, and it is also the core motivation for adjusting for covariates in the multivariable logistic regression models that follow.

title: Categorical data analysis
text:
Univariate Logistic regression

model3<-glm(formula = chd69~agec,family = binomial(link="logit"),data = data)
summary(model3)

#>

#>     data = data)

Exact logistic regression
Exact logistic regression is an extension of logistic regression in which log odds of the binary outcome is modeled as a linear combination of the predictor variables. It is used in the following situations:

When the sample size is too small for a regular logistic regression (which uses the standard maximum-likelihood-based estimator)
When some of the cells formed by the outcome and categorical predictor variable have zero observations.
When sample size is adequate but the event is rare (sparse data)
